name: Binge-eating disorder
dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Feeding and Eating Disorders — Binge-Eating Disorder
summary: Recurrent binge episodes with a felt loss of control and marked distress, without the regular vomiting, fasting or exercise used to undo them in bulimia. Episodes are often eaten alone and followed by shame, and many clients diet strictly between binges, which tends to keep the cycle going. It is the most common eating disorder in US adults and occurs at every body size. Eating-disorder-focused CBT, including guided self-help, is first line; weight-neutral language helps engagement. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask how often binges happen and for how long. See DSM-5-TR for frequency and duration guidance.

ruleOuts.label: Thyroid, gastrointestinal and endocrine illness
ruleOuts.note: Hyperthyroidism, diabetes, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease and other illnesses can cause weight change or eating changes; coordinate a medical work-up.

ruleOuts.label: Medication and substance effects
ruleOuts.note: Stimulants, some antidepressants, antipsychotics and other medicines change appetite and weight. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Depression and other mental health conditions
ruleOuts.note: Appetite loss in depression, food avoidance from fear of choking (ARFID) or contamination fears (OCD) can look similar; ask what drives the eating change.

specifiers.label: Severity by binge frequency (descriptive)
specifiers.note: Sets the last ICD-10-CM character (F50.810 to F50.813); F50.814 for remission. See DSM-5-TR for severity specifiers.

differentials.label: Bulimia nervosa
differentials.distinguishing: Regular vomiting, laxatives, fasting or hard exercise after binges.

differentials.label: Major depressive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Overeating with low mood but without discrete binge episodes and loss of control.

differentials.label: Night eating or other specified feeding or eating disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Eating mainly after waking at night, or a pattern below the binge-eating thresholds.

comorbidities.label: Adult ADHD
comorbidities.note: Impulsive eating and ADHD often co-occur; ask about attention history.

interventions.name: Eating-disorder-focused guided self-help
interventions.evidence: NICE NG69 recommends it as a first step for adults with binge-eating disorder.
interventions.note: CBT-based self-help with short supportive sessions.

interventions.name: Group or individual eating-disorder-focused CBT
interventions.evidence: NICE NG69 recommends it if self-help is not enough; Fairburn et al. (2009) supports CBT-E across eating disorders.
interventions.note: Regular eating, planned meals and snacks, and urge management.

interventions.name: Self-compassion and shame work
interventions.evidence: Shame maintains secrecy and binges; compassion-focused methods are an adjunct with growing evidence.

interventions.name: Medication referral
interventions.evidence: A prescriber may consider medication as an adjunct.
interventions.note: Prescribing decisions rest with the prescriber.

culturalNotes: Eating disorders occur across all genders, body sizes, ages, ethnic groups and income levels. Do not rule one out because the client is male, older, a person of color or in a larger body.

Food, fasting, body ideals and family meals carry cultural and religious meaning. Ask about religious fasting, cultural foods and family roles before planning meals, and adapt the plan rather than asking the client to drop practices that matter to them.
Weight stigma in health care is common. Use weight-neutral, respectful language and ask before weighing; consider blind weights where clinically appropriate.
Food insecurity can drive restriction followed by overeating. Ask about access to food and connect the client with food resources where needed.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, and check that key terms translate with the meaning you intend.
If the client wants faith or spiritual practice included, follow their lead and get informed consent first (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors); never impose beliefs.

redFlagRules.message: Medical warning signs related to eating are documented. Eating disorders carry real medical risk: arrange a same-day or urgent medical assessment (vital signs, electrolytes, ECG as indicated) and agree on a medical monitoring plan.

Suicidal thoughts or self-harm are documented in this input. Ask directly about intent, plan and access to means, follow your crisis protocol and build a safety plan with the client; this app never rates risk.
